narrativeReportMd:
# AdverseEvent R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
R6 keeps the AdverseEvent resource identity but substantially remodels the local content. Hard R4-to-R6 breaks include the new mandatory modifier `status`, several renamed or removed top-level elements, CodeableReference conversions, and a narrowed causality backbone.

## Scope
The analysis used the local R4 and R6 StructureDefinitions plus local value sets/code systems that are directly bound from AdverseEvent. Inherited Resource/DomainResource/Element changes are excluded and listed out of scope.

## Main migration themes
The largest theme is semantic remodeling rather than simple tightening: R4 `event`, `date`, `resultingCondition`, `contributor`, `subjectMedicalHistory`, and `referenceDocument` move to new names or more structured R6 concepts. The second theme is CodeableReference adoption, which changes JSON shape and enables concept-only data that R4 cannot represent. The third theme is terminology loosening/broadening, especially for category and outcome.

## Highest-impact findings
The mandatory modifier `status` must be populated for every migrated instance. `resultingCondition`, `contributor`, `subjectMedicalHistory`/`referenceDocument`, `suspectEntity.instance`, and `suspectEntity.causality` require explicit transform logic and, in several cases, clinical or implementation-guide policy. Top-level `severity` removal is clinically sensitive because no single local R6 replacement is present.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important where the correct mapping depends on clinical role: old history/document references may become supporting information, contributing factors, or actions; old severity may belong on a resulting Condition/Observation or an extension; multiple causality assessments need a merge/selection policy. Terminology findings also need review because SNOMED and external R6 code-system expansions were not available locally.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Many changes could have been staged with deprecated aliases or optional additions, but R6 appears to prefer a cleaner model with lifecycle status, participant roles, effect-oriented timing, and CodeableReference flexibility. Optional additions are forward-compatible but create R6-to-R4 data-loss risk.

## Follow-up analysis
Review CodeableReference conversion rules, official cross-version maps if available, and terminology expansions for the SNOMED and terminology.hl7.org value sets before implementing production transforms.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: AdverseEvent has multiple local hard breaking changes despite stable resource identity. Top concerns are mandatory modifier `status`, CodeableReference/participant/resulting-effect remodels, and clinically sensitive removal or splitting of severity/history/causality data. The largest uncertainty is exact terminology overlap for R6 SNOMED and external terminology bindings.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration is mostly a transformation exercise rather than a validator-only update. R4 fields must be renamed (`event` to `code`, `date` to `effectDateTime`), wrapped (`Reference` to `CodeableReference.reference`), classified into new semantic buckets (`supportingInfo`, `contributingFactor`, actions), or preserved by extension (`severity`, extra causality, R6-only fields). Reverse conversion from R6 to R4 is frequently lossy.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural and cardinality findings because both StructureDefinitions were present and directly compared. Confidence is medium for code-level terminology conclusions where R6 depends on SNOMED or external terminology.hl7.org content not expanded locally. Official diffs, narrative pages, and ConceptMaps could refine justification and mapping guidance but are unlikely to remove the main hard-breaking conclusions.

findings.title: R6 adds mandatory modifier element AdverseEvent.status

oldState.summary: R4 AdverseEvent has no lifecycle status element.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 instances have no local element that states whether the adverse event record is in progress, completed, entered in error, or unknown.

newState.summary: R6 requires AdverseEvent.status 1..1 as a modifier code bound to adverse-event-status.

binding.description: Codes identifying the lifecycle stage of an event.

flags.isModifierReason: This element is labeled as a modifier because it is a status element that contains status entered-in-error which means that the resource should not be treated as valid

newState.narrativeMd: R6 instances must carry one of in-progress, completed, entered-in-error, or unknown from the required value set.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct R4-to-R6 validation break because every R6 AdverseEvent must include status, while valid R4 instances cannot have that element. It is also a runtime risk because status is a modifier: generated models, validators, and business logic must not process entered-in-error events as ordinary clinical facts. R6-to-R4 conversion requires an extension or out-of-band metadata because R4 has no status slot.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Misinterpreting an entered-in-error adverse event as active clinical information can affect patient-safety or regulatory workflows.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding lifecycle status is a reasonable R6 goal because `entered-in-error` changes whether the event should be treated as valid clinical information. The breakage from making it mandatory is substantial, but an optional base element would leave generic R6 consumers unable to rely on seeing this safety-relevant modifier.
justification.inferredGoal: Add an explicit lifecycle state and entered-in-error handling to AdverseEvent.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Make `status` optional in base R6 and require it through profiles, warnings, or implementation guides.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could have introduced `AdverseEvent.status` as `0..1` with strong guidance or profiles requiring it. That would preserve existing R4 instances, but it only partially meets the R6 goal because absence of status would remain base-valid and downstream systems could not uniformly detect completed, in-progress, unknown, or entered-in-error events.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 instances but weakens the universal modifier signal for entered-in-error and lifecycle state.

evidence.detail: No AdverseEvent.status element exists in R4.
R6 defines status as 1..1 code, required binding, isModifier true.
R6 status value set includes in-progress, completed, entered-in-error, and unknown from event-status.

examples.examplesMd: The R4 example is a minimal illustrative instance fragment; the R6 migration adds the required lifecycle status.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 introduces a new mandatory lifecycle status on AdverseEvent. Because the element is required and modifier-significant, an R4 instance that otherwise has all required R4 fields will fail R6 validation until a status is supplied. The migration is not just syntactic: implementations must decide whether historical events are completed, still in progress, entered in error, or unknown.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Old-valid/new-invalid: any minimal R4 AdverseEvent with `actuality` and `subject` but no status is invalid in R6. Runtime compatibility is also affected for parsers and generated classes because R6 code must expose and honor the modifier element. R6-valid content cannot be represented in core R4 without an extension because R4 has no corresponding element.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Populate `AdverseEvent.status` during R4-to-R6 migration using reliable lifecycle metadata when available. Use `unknown` only when no better value exists, and treat `entered-in-error` as semantically significant. For R6-to-R4, preserve status in an extension or conversion sidecar and test downstream systems for entered-in-error handling.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The underlying need for lifecycle state appears reasonable, especially for entered-in-error semantics. A backward-compatible design could have added an optional status first and relied on profiles or warnings for requiredness, but that would leave base R6 consumers unable to rely on the field.

findings.title: AdverseEvent.event is renamed to AdverseEvent.code and its example value set changes

semanticText.short: Type of the event itself in relation to the subject
semanticText.definition: This element defines the specific type of event that occurred or that was prevented from occurring.

newState.summary: R6 uses optional AdverseEvent.code 0..1 CodeableConcept for the event or incident.

semanticText.short: Event or incident that occurred or was averted
semanticText.definition: Specific event that occurred or that was averted, such as patient fall, wrong organ removed, or wrong blood transfused.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The old and new elements have the same cardinality, datatype, binding name, and role as the specific adverse-event type; only the element name and descriptive text changed.

facts.note: The binding is example strength, but code-generation or pick-list behavior may still change.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a wire-format break for any instance that populates `event`: R6 validators reject unknown element `event`, while R4 validators reject unknown element `code`. Because the element is optional, instances that did not use it are unaffected, but generated model accessors, search code, serializers, and mapping rules must be updated.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Normalizing the primary adverse-event concept to the common `code` name is understandable, but this is an optional same-type rename. The R6 clinical goal could mostly have been met by clarifying the existing `event` definition or by staging a deprecated alias, so strict wire-format breakage is not clearly necessary.
justification.inferredGoal: Normalize the primary event concept element name to `code`.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `event` as the base element, or keep it deprecated while adding `code` as a preferred alias.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A backward-compatible base design could have kept `AdverseEvent.event` at `0..1 CodeableConcept` and updated its short/definition and terminology guidance, or added `AdverseEvent.code` while retaining `event` with an invariant or guidance that both must not diverge. This preserves R4-valid instances with only moderate long-term cost: either the model keeps a less conventional name or it carries duplicate concept representations during transition.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The main cost is carrying a non-preferred old name or temporarily reconciling duplicate `event`/`code` values.

evidence.detail: R4 defines event as 0..1 CodeableConcept with example binding to adverse-event-type.
R6 defines code as 0..1 CodeableConcept with the same binding name and event semantics.
The R4 example value set uses SNOMED clinical finding 404684003; the R6 value set uses adverse event 370894009 and code 1912002.

examples.examplesMd: The migration fragment shows the field-level rename; a complete R6 instance also needs `status`.

findings.narrativeMd: The primary event concept moved from `event` to `code`. Although the meaning is recognizable, the JSON property name and generated API name changed. Implementations that treat `event` as the clinical type of the adverse event need an explicit mapping to `code`, and terminology-driven UI lists may change because the example value set expression changed.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance containing `AdverseEvent.event` is not valid R6 JSON unless the value is moved to `code`. Conversely, R6 `code` content has no R4 property with the same name. The example binding means validators generally will not reject out-of-set codings, but generated enums, pick lists, and analytics keyed to the old path may break.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map `event` to `code` for R4-to-R6 and `code` back to `event` for R6-to-R4 when the value is a CodeableConcept. Review local terminology assumptions because the example SNOMED scope changed. Update FHIRPath expressions, search indexes, serializers, and generated accessor names.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A backward-compatible alternative was available: keep `event` and add `code` as an alias or preferred replacement with clear deprecation guidance. That would have avoided strict JSON breakage but would require duplicate-handling rules.

findings.title: AdverseEvent.date is replaced by choice element AdverseEvent.effect[x]

oldState.summary: R4 has optional AdverseEvent.date 0..1 dateTime for when the event occurred.

semanticText.definition: The date (and perhaps time) when the adverse event occurred.

newState.summary: R6 has optional AdverseEvent.effect[x] 0..1 with dateTime or Period for when the effect occurred.

semanticText.short: When the effect of the AdverseEvent occurred
semanticText.definition: The date (and perhaps time) when the effect of the AdverseEvent occurred.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The date/time occurrence field remains 0..1 and is the only top-level event/effect timing field, but R6 changes both the path and the allowed datatype domain.

facts.newValue: when the effect of the adverse event occurred

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances using `date` are invalid in R6 until transformed to `effectDateTime`. R6 also allows `effectPeriod`, which cannot be represented losslessly in the single R4 dateTime field. The wording changed from event occurrence to effect occurrence, so a syntactic rename may not be clinically correct in all cases.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of representing when the adverse effect occurred, including an interval, is clinically reasonable. A retained `date` would reduce validation breakage, but the R4 field's event-timing wording is not identical to the R6 effect-timing concept.
justification.inferredGoal: Represent the timing of the adverse effect and allow an interval.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Add effect timing while retaining deprecated `date` for legacy event/effect dateTime values.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have kept `AdverseEvent.date` as a deprecated `dateTime` and added `effect[x]` or an effect-period field for richer cases. That alternative protects common R4 instances but only partially meets the semantic cleanup goal because systems would need precedence and interpretation rules when both legacy event timing and new effect timing are present.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old payloads but leaves ambiguity between event timing and effect timing and creates overlapping timing fields.

evidence.detail: R4 date is 0..1 dateTime for when the adverse event occurred.
R6 effect[x] is 0..1 with dateTime and Period choices for when the effect occurred.

findings.narrativeMd: The top-level timing field changed name and became a choice. Existing R4 JSON with `date` must be rewritten to `effectDateTime`; R6 can now express a period of effect that R4 cannot hold directly. The semantic wording means migration code should not blindly assume all R4 event dates are effect dates when source systems distinguish exposure, detection, and effect timing.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Old-valid/new-invalid: `date` is not an R6 element. R6-valid `effectPeriod` is not cleanly representable in R4 because R4 only has one dateTime. Generated code changes from a scalar `date` property to a choice-type property, which can break serializers, FHIRPath, and API clients.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map R4 `date` to R6 `effectDateTime` only when the old value truly represented effect timing. When R6 has `effectPeriod`, preserve the interval in an extension or choose a lossy policy for R4 conversion. Update FHIRPath from `AdverseEvent.date` to `AdverseEvent.effect` / `effectDateTime` / `effectPeriod`.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A less-breaking path would have added `effect[x]` while retaining `date` as deprecated with guidance about precedence. That would avoid JSON breakage but carry two overlapping timing concepts.

findings.title: AdverseEvent.resultingCondition is replaced by CodeableReference AdverseEvent.resultingEffect

semanticText.short: Effect on the subject due to this event
semanticText.definition: Includes information about the reaction that occurred as a result of exposure to a substance.

newState.summary: R6 has resultingEffect 0..* CodeableReference(Condition|Observation) with example clinical-findings binding.

binding.description: Indicates the effect on subject due to this adverse event.

semanticText.short: Effect on the subject due to this event
semanticText.definition: Information about the condition that occurred as a result of the adverse event, such as hives due to exposure or a broken leg as a result of a fall.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The short description remains the effect on the subject and the old Condition reference target is still allowed through CodeableReference, but the path and JSON shape changed and Observation/concept-only representations were added.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This combines an element rename with a datatype-domain change. R4 JSON such as `resultingCondition: [{reference: ...}]` is invalid in R6; R6 expects `resultingEffect` entries with either `reference` or `concept` inside a CodeableReference. R6 Observation targets and concept-only effects cannot be represented in R4's Reference(Condition) field.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The resulting clinical effect is central to adverse-event interpretation; dropping or misclassifying it can alter clinical and reporting meaning.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Broadening resulting effects from Condition-only references to CodeableReference(Condition|Observation) and concept-only findings is a useful R6 improvement. The compatible design is incomplete because it would leave two same-resource ways to communicate a Condition effect.
justification.inferredGoal: Broaden resulting effects from Condition-only references to coded or referenced clinical findings.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain deprecated `resultingCondition` while adding `resultingEffect` for Observation and concept-only effects.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking transition could have kept `AdverseEvent.resultingCondition` as `0..* Reference(Condition)` and added `resultingEffect` for the broader R6 model. This would preserve R4 instances, but duplicate Condition-effect paths could diverge and deprecated representations might persist indefinitely, increasing validation and interoperability burden.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 Condition references but duplicates resulting-effect representation and requires conflict handling.

evidence.detail: R4 resultingCondition is 0..* Reference constrained to Condition.
R6 resultingEffect is 0..* CodeableReference constrained to Condition or Observation and bound to clinical-findings.
CodeableReference uses a nested `concept` or `reference`, so its JSON shape is not the same as a bare Reference.

examples.examplesMd: CodeableReference wraps a Reference inside its `reference` child; it is not the same JSON shape as R4's bare Reference.

findings.narrativeMd: The old result field was not merely renamed. R6 changes the representation from a list of Condition references to a list of CodeableReference values that may point to Condition, Observation, or carry only a concept. This expands the model but breaks both wire format and generated code.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `resultingCondition` become invalid in R6. R6 instances with `resultingEffect.reference` to Observation or `resultingEffect.concept` cannot be faithfully represented in R4 without creating or choosing a Condition, using an extension, or losing data.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4-to-R6, convert each Condition reference to `resultingEffect.reference`. For R6-to-R4, only Condition references map cleanly back. Observation references and concept-only entries need manual review, generated Condition resources, or extensions depending on the receiving system's rules.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A less disruptive design could have retained `resultingCondition` and added `resultingEffect` for broader cases. The tradeoff would be duplicate ways to express a Condition effect and possible inconsistencies.

findings.title: Top-level AdverseEvent.severity is removed

oldState.summary: R4 has optional AdverseEvent.severity 0..1 CodeableConcept with required mild/moderate/severe binding.

binding.description: The severity of the adverse event itself, in direct relation to the subject.

semanticText.definition: Describes the severity of the adverse event, in relation to the subject. Contrast to AdverseEvent.seriousness.

newState.summary: R6 has no top-level AdverseEvent.severity element.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 retains `seriousness` and describes severity in comments in relation to resulting effects, but the AdverseEvent resource no longer has this top-level severity property.

impact.impactRationaleMd: An R4 instance that includes `severity` is not valid against the R6 StructureDefinition. The removed element carried a required coded severity value, and the R6 resource does not provide a single local replacement slot, so migration is semantically lossy unless severity can be moved to a referenced Condition/Observation or extension.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Severity is clinically meaningful and can drive triage, regulatory reporting, and analytics; dropping it silently is unsafe.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Separating event seriousness from severity of the resulting clinical effect is a reasonable goal, but the supplied computable definitions do not show that removing the R4 severity slot was necessary. Because R6 has no direct local replacement, outright removal risks losing clinically significant mild/moderate/severe information.
justification.inferredGoal: Avoid conflating event seriousness with severity of a clinical effect.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain optional `severity` as deprecated with guidance to prefer severity on the resulting Condition or Observation.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could keep `AdverseEvent.severity` at `0..1 CodeableConcept`, mark it deprecated or legacy, and state that new R6 content should express effect severity on the resulting Condition or Observation where possible. This would preserve R4-valid instances with moderate tradeoff: legacy event-level severity might linger and need careful interpretation, but the R6 semantic clarification would still be available.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Keeps a legacy event-level severity field that may remain ambiguous, but preserves clinically important R4 data.

evidence.detail: R4 defines severity as 0..1 CodeableConcept with required adverse-event-severity binding.
No R6 element with this id exists.
R4 severity codes are mild, moderate, and severe.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment shows the removed R4 element; a complete R4 resource would also include required `actuality` and `subject`.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 removes the top-level severity element. This is a hard break for R4 payloads and code that stores adverse-event severity directly on the resource. The R6 model appears to prefer severity on the resulting clinical effect, but there is no computable one-step local target in AdverseEvent.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Old-valid/new-invalid: any R4 AdverseEvent with `severity` contains an unknown R6 property. This is primarily an R4-to-R6 validation and migration break. It does not create a direct R6-to-R4 local-field problem because R6 no longer carries this field, but R6 systems may express severity elsewhere in referenced resources.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not drop severity without policy. If the R4 severity describes a resulting Condition, consider populating `Condition.severity` on the referenced effect. If it is event-level severity, preserve it in an extension or implementation-guide-specific mapping and flag for clinical review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The removal might be semantically justified if severity belongs to a resulting condition rather than the adverse event itself. A backward-compatible alternative would have kept `severity` with deprecation guidance or provided an explicit replacement path.

findings.title: AdverseEvent.contributor is replaced by participant backbone entries

semanticText.definition: Parties that may or should contribute or have contributed information to the adverse event.

newState.summary: R6 participant is 0..* BackboneElement with optional function and required actor Reference with expanded targets.

semanticText.definition: Indicates who or what participated in the adverse event and how they were involved.

newState.narrativeMd: Each R6 participant has `actor` 1..1 and optional `function` bound by example to v3 ParticipationType codes INF, PART, WIT, and AUT.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: R6 participant generalizes the old contributor concept: the definition covers who participated and `function` can distinguish contributor or informant roles. The datatype and child structure are different.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a structural wire-format break: R4 stores a bare reference array, while R6 stores backbone objects with an `actor` child and optional role/function coding. R6 also allows actor target types that R4 contributor cannot carry. Code generated from R4 will not deserialize R6 participant objects as contributors, and R4 contributor properties disappear from R6 models.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 participant backbone reasonably captures who was involved and how, with broader actor types and optional function. A retained `contributor` shortcut would help old payloads but would not fully meet the role/function goal and would require reconciliation if both fields appeared.
justification.inferredGoal: Represent participants and their functions, not only contributors.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Add `participant` while retaining deprecated `contributor` as a shortcut for participant actor entries.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have retained `AdverseEvent.contributor` and mapped it to participant entries with absent or contributor-like `function`. This covers common R4 cases, but it only partially meets the R6 design because `participant.function` and expanded actor roles are central to the new model, and duplicate actor paths could accumulate indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves simple R4 references but duplicates participant representation and lacks function semantics on the old field.

evidence.detail: R4 contributor is 0..* Reference to Practitioner, PractitionerRole, or Device.
R6 participant is 0..* BackboneElement.
R6 participant.actor is required and targets Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Organization, CareTeam, Patient, Device, RelatedPerson, and Group.
R6 participant.function carries the type of involvement with an example binding.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 remodels contributors into a general participant backbone. Old contributor references should usually become `participant.actor`, but the role/function may need to be inferred. R6 can also represent witnesses, informants, organizations, care teams, patients, related persons, and groups in ways R4 contributor cannot directly encode.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 `contributor` entries are invalid in R6 because the element is gone. R6 `participant` entries are invalid in R4 without transformation and may be impossible to reduce to R4 when the actor target is outside the old target set or when function semantics matter.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4-to-R6, create one `participant` per `contributor`, copy the reference to `actor`, and populate `function` only when source data supports a reliable code. For R6-to-R4, only actor references to Practitioner, PractitionerRole, or Device map cleanly; preserve other actors and functions in extensions or reject with review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A less breaking approach would have kept `contributor` as an alias for participant entries with contributor-like function. That would ease old data migration but leave two paths for similar information.

findings.title: Subject history and reference documents are split into supportingInfo, contributingFactor, and action fields

oldState.summary: R4 has subjectMedicalHistory 0..* Reference(...) and referenceDocument 0..* Reference(DocumentReference).
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 separates a broad `subjectMedicalHistory` reference list from a `referenceDocument` list.

newState.summary: R6 uses multiple 0..* CodeableReference fields: supportingInfo, contributingFactor, preventiveAction, and mitigatingAction.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 distinguishes supporting information from contributing factors and preventive or mitigating actions; each can carry a coded concept or a reference to selected resource types.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The R6 `supportingInfo` definition explicitly covers subject medical history and relevant documents, while new `contributingFactor`, `preventiveAction`, and `mitigatingAction` fields split out information that might previously have appeared as history or documents. The mapping depends on the clinical role of each reference.

newValue: MedicationAdministration, MedicationStatement, MedicationRequest, Device, QuestionnaireResponse appear in selected new fields; Media is not listed

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 elements `subjectMedicalHistory` and `referenceDocument` are absent in R6, so old payloads using them fail strict R6 validation. The replacement is not one-to-one: R6 requires choosing whether each item is supporting information, a contributing factor, a preventive action, or a mitigating action. R6 CodeableReference concept-only entries and several new target types cannot be represented directly in R4.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Classifying a condition as merely supporting history versus a contributing factor can change clinical interpretation and adverse-event analysis.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Separating supporting information from contributing factors and preventive or mitigating actions is a meaningful modeling improvement. The less-breaking path would preserve old instances, but it would also keep broad catch-all fields that obscure the distinction R6 is trying to make.
justification.inferredGoal: Separate background history/documents from factors and actions related to the adverse event.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `subjectMedicalHistory` and `referenceDocument` while adding the more specific R6 CodeableReference fields.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A transitional base design could keep the R4 history/document reference lists as deprecated and add `supportingInfo`, `contributingFactor`, `preventiveAction`, and `mitigatingAction`. That alternative is incomplete because the old buckets cannot express the R6 clinical role and may conflict with the new buckets, requiring duplicate-detection and classification rules.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old broad buckets but weakens the semantic split and creates duplicate or conflicting classifications.

evidence.detail: R4 subjectMedicalHistory is a broad Reference list including Condition, Observation, AllergyIntolerance, FamilyMemberHistory, Immunization, Procedure, Media, and DocumentReference.
R4 referenceDocument is 0..* Reference(DocumentReference).
R6 supportingInfo is CodeableReference and its definition explicitly covers subject medical history and relevant documents.
R6 contributingFactor captures factors suspected to increase probability or severity.
R6 preventiveAction captures actions that helped avoid the adverse event.
R6 mitigatingAction captures actions taken after the event to reduce harm.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 replaces two broad R4 reference lists with several semantically narrower CodeableReference lists. This is one of the more migration-sensitive changes because the correct target field depends on why the referenced item matters. A historical penicillin allergy might be supporting information in one record and a contributing factor in another, depending on the event narrative.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Old-valid/new-invalid: R4 payloads with `subjectMedicalHistory` or `referenceDocument` contain unknown R6 elements. R6-to-R4 is lossy for concept-only CodeableReferences, new target types, and distinctions among supporting, contributing, preventive, and mitigating information, because R4 has only broader buckets.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Build mapping rules that classify each R4 reference by clinical role. Defaulting all history and documents to `supportingInfo.reference` is syntactically easy but may understate causality or actions. Preserve unclassifiable roles in extensions and include clinical review cases for causal factors, preventive actions, and mitigating actions.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A backward-compatible transition could have kept `subjectMedicalHistory` and `referenceDocument` while adding the new R6 fields. The tradeoff would be ambiguity and possible duplicate information across old and new buckets.

findings.title: suspectEntity.instance changes from Reference to CodeableReference with expanded targets

oldState.summary: R4 suspectEntity.instance is required Reference to Immunization, Procedure, Substance, Medication, MedicationAdministration, MedicationStatement, or Device.

newState.summary: R6 suspectEntity.instance is required CodeableReference to the old targets plus SubstanceDefinition, BiologicallyDerivedProduct, and ResearchStudy.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Although the path and cardinality are unchanged, the JSON representation changed. A bare R4 Reference object under `instance` is not a valid R6 CodeableReference; R6 expects `instance.reference` or `instance.concept`. R6 can also name a suspect entity by concept only or by new target types that R4 cannot carry.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The suspect entity is central to adverse-event causality; losing it can undermine safety analysis and regulatory reporting.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Supporting coded suspect entities and additional targets is a strong R6 goal, especially when no concrete resource instance exists. A less-breaking design could preserve the bare Reference shape for R4 instances, but it would not provide the same unified CodeableReference pattern.
justification.inferredGoal: Support coded suspect entities and more target resource types.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `instance` as Reference and add a concept-valued sibling or choice for non-resource suspect entities.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have widened the existing Reference target list and added a separate coded suspect-entity element for concept-only cases. This would preserve R4-valid JSON, but the alternative is only partial because concept and reference forms would be separate fields for the same fact, with potential conflicts and extra implementation burden compared with one CodeableReference element.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Avoids wrapping old references but splits suspect-entity representation and creates consistency risks.

evidence.detail: R4 instance is 1..1 Reference with seven target profiles.
R6 instance is 1..1 CodeableReference with ten target profiles.
CodeableReference can carry `concept` or nested `reference`, changing JSON shape from a bare Reference.

findings.narrativeMd: The suspect entity field keeps its name but changes type. This is easy to miss because the path is stable, but it is a hard serialization and code-generation break: the old `Reference.reference` property is now nested one level deeper inside CodeableReference.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Old-valid/new-invalid: R4 `suspectEntity.instance` as a bare Reference is invalid in R6. R6-valid concept-only suspect entities or references to SubstanceDefinition, BiologicallyDerivedProduct, or ResearchStudy cannot be represented in the R4 field. Generated models must change the property type even though the element name did not change.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Wrap R4 references as `suspectEntity.instance.reference` during R4-to-R6 conversion. For R6-to-R4, unwrap only if the CodeableReference has a supported Reference target. Preserve concept-only values or newly allowed target types using extensions or manual review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A backward-compatible alternative was to make `instance[x]` allow both Reference and CodeableReference-like concept representation or to add a sibling coded element. That would reduce JSON breakage but increase model complexity.

findings.title: suspectEntity.causality is limited to one entry and its children are renamed or removed

oldState.summary: R4 causality is 0..* with assessment, productRelatedness, author, and method children.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 can carry multiple causality assessments per suspect entity and includes free-text `productRelatedness`.

newState.summary: R6 causality is 0..1 with assessmentMethod, entityRelatedness, and author; author targets are expanded.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 allows only one causality backbone, renames method/assessment, removes productRelatedness, and allows Patient or RelatedPerson as author.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The parent path is unchanged and child definitions line up by causality role, but the maximum cardinality and child identities changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The max cardinality reduction is a direct validation break for any R4 suspect entity with more than one causality entry. Even a single R4 causality entry must be renamed internally, and `productRelatedness` has no local R6 child. R6-to-R4 conversion also loses Patient/RelatedPerson author targets.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Causality assessment drives whether a product, medication, or action is treated as responsible for harm; collapsing multiple assessments can change interpretation.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Clarifying causality child names is reasonable, but the computable evidence does not justify reducing `causality` from many entries to one or removing legacy fields in a way that can discard independent assessments. The most breaking part appears avoidable unless R6 intentionally requires a single authoritative causality statement, which is not shown here.
justification.inferredGoal: Simplify and clarify causality assessment structure.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep causality repeatable and preserve old child names as aliases or deprecated fields while adding clearer names.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could keep `AdverseEvent.suspectEntity.causality` at `0..*`, retain `assessment`, `method`, and `productRelatedness` as deprecated or alias fields, and add clearer `entityRelatedness` and `assessmentMethod` guidance. This preserves R4-valid instances and still supports clearer R6 semantics, at the manageable cost of a larger backbone and alias-handling rules.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Maintains a more complex backbone, but avoids data loss for multiple clinically meaningful causality assessments.

evidence.detail: R4 causality is 0..*.
R6 causality is 0..1.
R4 has productRelatedness 0..1 string.
R6 has entityRelatedness 0..1 CodeableConcept using the causality assessment value set.
R6 has assessmentMethod 0..1 CodeableConcept using the causality method value set.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example selects one assessment; real migrations should not discard additional assessments without policy.

findings.narrativeMd: The causality component is narrowed and renamed. The most concrete validation break is the max decrease from many to one; the subtler break is that old child names and a free-text relatedness field are gone. Migrations must decide how to merge or choose among multiple assessments.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with two causality entries under one suspect entity are invalid in R6. R4 child fields `assessment`, `method`, and `productRelatedness` are not R6 fields. R6 entries authored by Patient or RelatedPerson cannot be represented in the R4 author target list.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For each suspect entity, map `assessment` to `entityRelatedness` and `method` to `assessmentMethod`. If there are multiple causality entries, define a deterministic selection, merge strategy, or preserve extras in extensions. Map `productRelatedness` to CodeableConcept text, note, or extension only with review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A compatibility-preserving design could have retained repeatability and old child aliases while adding clearer R6 names. That would preserve data but maintain a more complex backbone.

findings.title: AdverseEvent.category binding weakens from extensible to example and the category vocabulary appears to shift

oldState.summary: R4 category is 0..* CodeableConcept with extensible binding to adverse-event-category.

binding.description: Overall categorization of the event, e.g. product-related or situational.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R4 local CodeSystem content was available; R6 external CodeSystem content was not present locally, so code-level comparison is partial.

newState.summary: R6 category remains 0..* CodeableConcept but binding strength is example.

binding.description: Overall categorization of the event, e.g. product-related or situational.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: Added codes are inferred from the R6 element short text, not a locally available complete CodeSystem expansion.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Weakening extensible to example is not an R4-to-R6 validation break; it relaxes conformance. However, systems that relied on the R4 category code set for validation, routing, dashboards, or decision support may observe changed semantics. R6 categories may not map cleanly back to the R4 product/problem-oriented list.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Loosening category terminology and updating the example categories is plausibly intended to support broader categorization. Exact code-level rationale remains limited without the external R6 terminology expansion, but the change is not a strict R4-to-R6 validation break because old CodeableConcept values remain structurally allowed.
justification.inferredGoal: Loosen category terminology and update category concepts.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the binding is weakened to example and does not invalidate R4 category instances.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No less-breaking base R6 design is needed to preserve R4 instances because the R6 binding is weaker, not stronger. A ConceptMap or retained compatibility value set would help migration and analytics, but that is terminology guidance for semantic consistency rather than a backwards-compatible base-design alternative.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The remaining risk is semantic and downgrade mapping ambiguity, not preservation of old R4 instances in R6.

evidence.detail: R4 category binding strength is extensible.
R6 category binding strength is example.
R4 local CodeSystem includes product-problem, product-quality, product-use-error, wrong-dose, and related product/use-error codes.
R6 short text lists wrong-patient, procedure-mishap, medication-mishap, device, unsafe-physical-environment, hospital-aquired-infection, and wrong-body-site.

examples.examplesMd: No compact example is included; the evidence and migration text describe the affected JSON shape.

findings.narrativeMd: The category element remains structurally present, but its conformance expectations change. R4 required use of the value set when an applicable code existed; R6 only provides examples. The visible category list also shifts from product/use-error categories toward patient/procedure/medication/device mishap categories.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: This is not a strict R4-to-R6 instance break. Existing R4 category codings can still appear in CodeableConcept. The risk is semantic and operational: R6 validators will not enforce the old extensible requirement, and R6 category values may not satisfy R4 extensible expectations or local analytics built on the R4 code set.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not assume category code semantics are unchanged. Review dashboards, search filters, decision rules, and profile bindings that depended on the R4 category set. A ConceptMap or site-specific mapping table is likely needed for old product-use categories versus newer mishap categories.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: If the goal was to broaden terminology, retaining extensible strength with a broader value set or publishing an explicit ConceptMap would have been more migration-friendly. Weakening to example avoids validation failures but can reduce interoperability guarantees.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: A complete comparison needs the external terminology.hl7.org R6 CodeSystem or expansion; only R4 local concepts and R6 element text were available.

findings.title: AdverseEvent.outcome becomes repeatable and changes from required local codes to example SNOMED binding

oldState.summary: R4 outcome is 0..1 CodeableConcept with required binding to six adverse-event-outcome codes.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R4 had a small complete local CodeSystem; R6 uses a SNOMED expression and no local expansion was performed.

newState.summary: R6 outcome is 0..* CodeableConcept with example binding to SNOMED descendants of 405533003.

binding.description: Codes describing the type of outcome from the adverse event.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R6 compose includes SNOMED descendent-of 405533003; expansion was not available locally.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4-to-R6 validation is relaxed and max cardinality increases, so existing R4 outcome values are not made invalid by structure alone. The major risk is reverse conversion and generated code: R6 can carry multiple outcomes and SNOMED-coded outcomes outside the six-code R4 required value set, neither of which fits R4 cleanly.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Allowing multiple and richer outcome concepts is reasonable, especially given the R4 binding description questioned requiredness. This does not make existing R4 outcome instances invalid in R6; the main impact is that new R6 outcomes may not fit R4's single required-code slot.
justification.inferredGoal: Allow richer and multiple outcome concepts.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: outcome cardinality and terminology are widened, preserving R4-to-R6 validity.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Because the R6 base change widens max cardinality and weakens the binding, there is no less-breaking R4-to-R6 design to identify. Official ConceptMaps or compatibility guidance would reduce R6-to-R4 ambiguity, but they are migration aids rather than base alternatives for preserving old instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Multiple or SNOMED-coded R6 outcomes create downgrade loss, but that is not an R4-preservation alternative.

evidence.detail: R4 outcome is 0..1 and required-bound to adverse-event-outcome|4.0.1.
R6 outcome is 0..* and example-bound to adverse-event-outcome.
R4 local codes are resolved, recovering, ongoing, resolvedWithSequelae, fatal, and unknown.
R6 compose uses SNOMED descendent-of 405533003.

examples.examplesMd: The SNOMED code is illustrative because no local SNOMED expansion was available.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 widens `outcome` in two dimensions: cardinality and terminology. That is friendly to new R6 data capture, but it breaks assumptions in R4 clients that there is at most one outcome and that the value is one of the six R4 codes.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances remain structurally valid after straightforward R4-to-R6 conversion. R6 instances with multiple outcomes or SNOMED outcomes cannot be represented losslessly in R4. Strict R4 validators will reject non-R4 outcome codes because the old binding is required.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4, define a selection or prioritization rule when multiple outcomes exist, and map SNOMED outcomes to one of the R4 codes only where clinically defensible. Preserve unmapped or additional outcomes in extensions or reject with manual review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R4 TODO-like binding description suggests the required binding may have been too restrictive. A less disruptive path would have included an official ConceptMap and perhaps retained the old value set as a preferred compatibility layer.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: SNOMED expansion was not available, so exact overlap with the six R4 outcome codes was not determined.

findings.title: AdverseEvent.actuality required value set adds code unknown

oldState.summary: R4 actuality is required code with allowed codes actual and potential.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R4 local CodeSystem was complete for actual and potential.

newState.summary: R6 actuality is still required and modifier, but adds unknown.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The local R6 CodeSystem adds unknown and says the source system does not specify which value applies.

facts.newValue: unknown is included to support legacy data and is strongly discouraged

impact.impactRationaleMd: Existing R4 `actual` and `potential` values remain valid in R6, so this is not an old-data validation break. New R6 `unknown` values are not valid in R4's required two-code value set, and enum-based R4 clients may fail when reading R6 data.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 comment says `unknown` is included for legacy data and strongly discouraged, which is a plausible compatibility goal. Since existing R4 values remain valid, the change is not a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design issue.
justification.inferredGoal: Permit legacy records where actual versus potential is unknown.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: adding `unknown` widens the required value set and keeps R4 `actual` and `potential` valid.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No R4-preserving alternative is needed for forward compatibility. A data-absent-reason or profile extension could avoid introducing a new base code for downgrade consumers, but that would make the unknown state less visible in R6 and addresses R6-to-R4 compatibility rather than preserving R4 instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R4 enum and downgrade handling are affected, but extension-only handling would optimize reverse compatibility rather than avoid an R4-to-R6 break.

evidence.detail: R4 actuality binding is required to adverse-event-actuality|4.0.1.
R4 codes are actual and potential.
R6 says unknown is included to support legacy data and is strongly discouraged.
R6 adds unknown.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment isolates the required code change.

findings.narrativeMd: The required `actuality` element remains at the same path and still has actual/potential semantics, but R6 adds an `unknown` code. This is a widening for R6 and a reverse-conversion problem for R4.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 compatibility is good for existing values. R6-to-R4 is not clean when `actuality='unknown'` because R4 requires the element and does not permit that code. R4 enum switches should add a defensive path if they ingest R6 data.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: When converting R6 `unknown` to R4, avoid inventing `actual` or `potential` unless source evidence supports it. Preserve the R6 code in an extension or reject for manual completion. Test enum parsing for the new code.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Using an extension would have preserved R4 required-code compatibility but made the unknown state less integrated into base R6. The R6 comment suggests the change is intentionally narrow and discouraged.

findings.title: AdverseEvent.identifier maximum cardinality increases from 1 to many

impact.impactRationaleMd: Increasing max cardinality does not invalidate R4 instances in R6. It does change generated code from a scalar/single optional value to a collection in R6, and R6 instances with multiple identifiers cannot be represented losslessly in R4.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Supporting multiple business identifiers is consistent with the element comment and common FHIR identifier patterns. The widening is forward-compatible for existing R4 data, though generated R6 models and downgrade conversions must handle a collection.
justification.inferredGoal: Support multiple business identifiers for an adverse event.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: increasing `identifier` max from 1 to * preserves all R4 instances.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Because the base cardinality is widened, no less-breaking design is needed to preserve R4 instances. Keeping max `1` would improve R4 round-tripping but would block the R6 expressivity goal rather than avoid a forward compatibility break.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The tradeoff is R6-to-R4 identifier selection or extension handling, not an R4-to-R6 validation break.

evidence.detail: R4 identifier max is 1.
R6 identifier max is *.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment is R6-local; R4 can carry only one `identifier`.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 allows multiple business identifiers. This is not a breaking change for old R4 data, but it is a code-generation and reverse-mapping risk because R4 models often expose a single identifier property.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 is safe for single identifiers. R6-to-R4 requires choosing one identifier, using an extension, or producing multiple related resources, any of which can lose or distort identity information.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update generated R6 models and serializers to treat `identifier` as a collection. For R6-to-R4, establish a priority order by system/use or preserve additional identifiers in extensions.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A less disruptive approach would have left max 1 and relied on profiles for repetitions, but that would limit base R6 expressivity and is less aligned with FHIR identifier patterns.

findings.title: R6 adds optional local fields with no direct R4 home

oldState.summary: R4 has no expectedInResearchStudy, note, or suspectEntity.occurrence[x] fields.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 also lacks the R6 action-specific CodeableReference fields except through broader history/document references or extensions.

newState.summary: R6 adds expectedInResearchStudy 0..1 boolean, note 0..* Annotation, and suspectEntity.occurrence[x] 0..1 dateTime|Period, plus action-oriented fields.
newState.narrativeMd: These optional additions do not block R4-to-R6 validation but can carry information that core R4 cannot represent.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Optional additions are not old-instance breaking. They are material for round-trip and migration because R6 can record study expectation, comments, suspect-entity timing, and action-specific details that have no exact R4 element.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding optional fields for research expectation, notes, suspect-entity occurrence, and action details improves R6 expressivity without creating an R4-to-R6 validation break. The compatibility concern is only that new R6 content may lack a native R4 home.
justification.inferredGoal: Increase expressivity for study expectation, notes, suspect-entity timing, and actions.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: these are optional additive R6 fields and do not invalidate R4 instances.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No less-breaking forward design is required for optional additions. Keeping these concepts only in extensions would simplify R4 round-tripping, but it would reduce their discoverability and consistency in the R6 base resource.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R4 extensions or sidecars support downgrade, but they are mitigations rather than less-breaking base R6 alternatives.

evidence.detail: R6 adds expectedInResearchStudy 0..1 boolean.
R6 adds note 0..* Annotation.
R6 adds suspectEntity occurrence dateTime or Period.
No matching R4 elements exist for these paths.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds several optional data-bearing elements. They do not make R4 instances invalid in R6, but once R6 systems use them, a core R4 receiver has no direct place for the data. This is especially relevant for research-trial workflows (`expectedInResearchStudy`) and timing of the suspect exposure or entity.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 is not broken by these additions. R6-to-R4 conversion is potentially lossy: notes could be dropped or moved to extensions, suspect-entity occurrence has no R4 slot, and expected-in-study status has no R4 boolean equivalent.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Define cross-version extensions or profile-specific mappings for each new field before round-tripping R6 data to R4. Do not silently discard research expectation or suspect-entity timing if they are part of downstream safety or trial reporting workflows.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Adding optional fields is the usual backward-compatible mechanism for forward evolution. The remaining risk is not avoidability of the R6 additions but the lack of standard R4 representation in the supplied inputs.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: Canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, derivation, baseDefinition, and abstract flag are stable. The status metadata changes from draft to active but does not change instance shape.

For unchanged local reference elements, `subject`, `encounter`, `location`, `recorder`, and `study` retain their R4 target profile sets. Reference target changes that are part of remodels are reported separately.
No AdverseEvent-specific invariant was added or strengthened. Observed dom/ele/ext constraint expression changes are inherited/base-artifact concerns and excluded from findings.
No local fixed, pattern, or default value constraints were found on AdverseEvent elements in either version.
No local maxLength, regex, minValue, or maxValue restrictions were identified as changing for AdverseEvent.
No local slicing rules were found on AdverseEvent elements in either StructureDefinition.
Existing local `actuality` remains a modifier; the new modifier `status` is reported as a finding. Inherited `implicitRules` and `modifierExtension` details are out of scope.
Existing local clinical elements did not show material isSummary flips. R6 adds explicit `mustSupport:false` metadata broadly, which does not create a support obligation.

No resource-level serialization format change was found beyond the element names and datatype shape changes reported in findings. CodeableReference conversions are reported where local elements use them.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Resource metadata status changes from draft to active
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The artifact status metadata affects standards maturity and publication interpretation, not instance validation shape by itself.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Governance processes may treat active R6 AdverseEvent as more mature than R4 draft, but implementations still need to handle the structural breaking changes separately.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: seriousness narrative is clarified
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The path, cardinality, datatype, and example binding for `seriousness` remain stable. R6 clarifies the distinction between seriousness and severity/effect examples.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Review business rules that conflated seriousness with removed top-level severity; the structural break is on `severity`, not `seriousness`.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: study definition changes from placeholder to explicit research-study enrollment text
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The element remains 0..* Reference(ResearchStudy). Only short/definition text is improved from placeholder wording.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: The clarified text may help implementers interpret existing study references but does not require a data transform.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Several high-impact AdverseEvent changes depend on Reference-to-CodeableReference conversion and concept-only representability rules.
R6 uses SNOMED and external terminology bindings for several fields. Expansion and ConceptMap analysis are needed for production-grade terminology migration.
Inherited language, contained-resource invariant, extension, and backbone metadata changes were observed but intentionally excluded under the base-artifact scope rule.
Search parameter names and expressions likely changed alongside local element renames such as date/effect and event/code, but search parameters are out of this artifact-structure report scope.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No official R4-to-R6 diff or ballot change log was available locally, so justification assessments are inferred from StructureDefinition content and terminology only.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Use official HL7 change notes, Jira items, or generated cross-version diff pages.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: SNOMED-based value sets and R6 external terminology.hl7.org CodeSystems were not expanded or fully available locally. Findings involving category, outcome, type, and action value sets therefore identify binding expressions and apparent code-list shifts rather than complete code-by-code deltas.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Run terminology expansion against the relevant R4 and R6 value sets with versioned SNOMED and terminology.hl7.org content, then compare expansions and official ConceptMaps.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Narrative specification pages and implementation guidance were not inspected, so semantic migration recommendations may miss explanatory text outside the computable package artifacts.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Review the R4 and R6 AdverseEvent narrative pages and any Patient Care work group notes.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Inline JSON examples are minimal illustrative fragments focused on changed fields. They were not submitted to a full FHIR validator with all required surrounding resources and terminology services.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Create full R4 and R6 fixture instances and validate them with version-specific validators and terminology support.

crossArtifactPatternsToCheck: R4 required terminology bindings weakened to example in R6
dateTime fields changed to dateTime|Period choice elements
